name: Funder Formatting and Compliance
title: Funder Formatting and Compliance
answer: Funder formatting and compliance covers the rules a funding body sets for how a proposal must be written, assembled, and submitted, including page limits, font and margin requirements, section order, citation style, budget justification, biosketches, and required attachments. It also covers the non-format rules that travel with a proposal, such as eligibility, cost principles, data management plans, ethics approvals, and reporting obligations. For an AI researcher, the scope often includes special clauses on compute costs, model documentation, data provenance, and open access to code or weights. The work sits between the research idea and the funder's administrative review, so it touches both the science and the institution's research office.

It also covers the non-format rules that travel with a proposal, such as eligibility, cost principles, data management plans, ethics approvals, and reporting obligations. For an AI researcher, the scope often includes special clauses on compute costs, model documentation, data provenance, and open access to code or weights. The work sits between the research idea and the funder's administrative review, so it touches both the science and the institution's research office.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the funder's submission portal, the institution's grants management system, and ordinary document tools such as word processors, reference managers, and PDF exporters. Templates and checklists from the funder or research office define the required structure, while spreadsheets and budgeting systems hold the numbers that must match across narrative, budget, and justification. Version control and shared drives matter because multiple authors, department administrators, and compliance officers may edit the same package. Some institutions also use automated validation tools that check page counts, file names, and required fields before submission.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method is a staged review: read the funding call, map every required section to a template, draft the science, then run a compliance pass against the funder's checklist. Writers track page limits, font sizes, margins, citation formats, and attachment naming rules, and they reconcile the budget narrative with the budget table. Institutional research administrators often review eligibility, cost allowability, subaward details, and required disclosures before the proposal is routed for signature. For AI projects, the method may also include documenting datasets, model training details, compute resources, and evaluation methods in the format the funder expects.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on the funder's terms, the institution's policies, and the accuracy of what is submitted. Proposal content may be treated as confidential during review, but award terms can require public access to publications, data, or software, and they can define who owns resulting intellectual property. Risks include rejection for formatting errors, audit findings for misstated costs, and reputational or legal exposure for plagiarism, fabricated preliminary data, or undisclosed conflicts. Provenance matters for every claim, citation, biosketch entry, and preliminary result, and many funders now require disclosure of generative AI use in drafting. Practices vary, so the governing documents are the funding call, the award conditions, and the institution's research policies.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward machine-readable proposals, automated compliance checks, and structured data for budgets, biosketches, and outputs. Funders are increasingly asking for persistent identifiers, data management and sharing plans, and open metadata that can be validated at submission rather than after review. AI-assisted drafting is likely to become more common, with corresponding rules about disclosure, accuracy, and confidentiality of unpublished ideas. For AI researchers, the horizon also includes clearer expectations for compute reporting, model cards, dataset documentation, and reproducibility artifacts. Formatting and compliance will remain administrative work, but more of it will be encoded in templates and validation systems.
